[6] The RPD found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the same-sex relationship with XXXX in Kenya, as alleged. This finding was based on inconsistent evidence about the duration of the relationship and whether it was known to XXXX brother, as well as inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's description of the relationship. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by incorrectly characterizing as inconsistent the evidence describing the relationship and by incorrectly finding omissions. I am not persuaded by these arguments. I find that the RPD assessed the evidence correctly. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged. My reasons follow.

[7] The Appellant testified that he had a same-sex relationship with XXXX for about a year and a half.2 In subsequent testimony, he stated that the relationship began in 1996 and ended around 2006.3 Asked to explain the inconsistency in his testimony, the Appellant stated that the relationship was off and on and he cannot say what the duration was.4 The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. I agree. If the relationship was off and on over a period of ten years, this does not explain why the Appellant would testify that the relationship lasted for a year and a half. The Appellant has not taken issue with the RPD's finding on this inconsistency. I find no error in the RPD's conclusion that this is an inconsistency that undermines the credibility of the Appellant's evidence about this relationship.

[8] The Appellant provided a letter from XXXX brother to corroborate the relationship.5 The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with the letter. The Appellant's testimony was that XXXX died and XXXX brother contacted him to let him know.6 He testified XXXX brother knew that they were friends but never knew about their relationship.7 In the letter, XXXX brother states that, at XXXX send-off, the Appellant told him that they had a sexual relationship. Asked to explain why the brother would say that, the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Yeah, yeah. That one I did not want to use that one because I - I never - no - nobody told him that we had a sexual relationship, but during his send-off I remember I mentioned something like that to him.8
The panel asked the Appellant why he had previously testified that the brother did not know, and the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Because of how - how hard is in Kenya, when you declare yourself the sexual orientation that you are in like you are bisexual, I - I did not because of that fear. Maybe that is why I never told you before that I had told him - I - I had told him.9
The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation. I agree. The Appellant has not addressed this inconsistency in his arguments. I find no error in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. I have considered Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE Guideline).10 In particular, I have taken into account the challenges claimants may face in disclosing their sexual orientation, including psychological barriers. I do not find that this explains why the Appellant would testify at the RPD that the brother never knew about the relationship. The inconsistency that arose at the hearing was because he testified that he had not disclosed his relationship with XXXX to the brother.

[9] The brother's letter also states that XXXX died in a road accident in 2012. The Appellant testified that he found out about XXXX death in 2010.11 When questioned about the inconsistency, the Appellant testified that it might have been 2012.12 Given that the Appellant testified that he had attended the send-off, the panel asked him to explain, given the evidence that in 2012 he was in Afghanistan. The Appellant first said he was not in Afghanistan, then said that he was, and that every six months he was given a few days off and he would return to Nairobi.13 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved when he was confronted with inconsistencies between his testimony and other evidence and that this undermines his credibility as a witness.

[10] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about how he and XXXX spent time together was inconsistent. In his BOC, the Appellant's evidence is that they had a sexual relationship and they would rent rooms at hotels for sex or have sex in storage rooms at their workplace.14 The evidence in his BOC is that he was forced to resign his job because they were discovered together in a storage room.15 In his testimony, the Appellant said that he had a key to XXXX place, they used to hang out there together, they used to go to bars together, and they had a relationship.16 When the panel referred the Appellant to the evidence in his BOC and asked him why they would have sex at work or rent hotel rooms if they could go to XXXX place, the Appellant testified that it was for a change of atmosphere.17 The Appellant argues that there is no inconsistency in his evidence as his testimony constitutes elaborative details so it is incorrect to draw a negative credibility inference. He argues that the finding of inconsistency is based on the sparseness of the BOC and the style of the writing and it is an error to conclude that the Appellant described the relationship differently in his testimony. I am not persuaded by this argument. In his BOC, the Appellant described the relationship with XXXX as a sexual relationship that involved having sex at work. His testimony is that the relationship was more than a sexual one. I find this inconsistent. I also find his explanation that they rented hotel rooms for a change of atmosphere is not reasonable. However, if I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in finding this evidence inconsistent, for purposes of the analysis, I still conclude that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged, based on the findings that the Appellant has not challenged and that I have already discussed.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents

[11] The RPD found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in dismissing documents as non-genuine without considering what they say. I am not persuaded by this argument. The Federal Court has said that a letter that is not authentic has zero weight.18 The panel did not err in giving no weight to documents that were found to be non-genuine. On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant submitted documents that, on a balance of probabilities, are not genuine. My reasons follow.
The RPD correctly found that the school letters are not genuine documents

[12] The Appellant provided two letters in support of his allegation that he was expelled from two XXXX XXXX because, in each case, he was caught engaging in sexual activity with another male student. The RPD found that these letters were not authentic documents. On an independent assessment, I find no error in this and I reach the same conclusion. My reasons follow.

[13] The Appellant's evidence in his BOC was that in XXXX 1995 he was caught in sexual activity in an empty classroom, called to the principal's office on the same day, and expelled on the spot.19 In a letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 1995, the school principal states that he received a report on XXXX XXXX, 1995 on the Appellant's behaviour, he set up a panel with board members, the panel reached "an anonymous decision" to expel the Appellant, and the Appellant was "hereby expelled".20 Asked to explain the inconsistency between the letter and his BOC, the Appellant replied "Yeah, he - he expelled me on the spot, but it is after they met with [the] Board of Governors."21 The Appellant argues that he testified that he was expelled on the spot after the board of governors met. I do not accept this argument nor do I find his explanation for the inconsistency reasonable. It does not reasonably explain the discrepancy between the evidence in his BOC that he was called to the principal's office on the day he was caught and expelled on the spot, and the evidence in the letter that he was expelled two days later.

[18] The letters in question, with accompanying identity documents, are from the Appellant's alleged same-sex partners in XXXX XXXX, XXXX26 and XXXX,27 and the brother of his alleged same-sex partner XXXX .28 The RPD found that the identity cards differ from other identity cards provided and from samples in the objective evidence. The panel found that, on the three cards in question, the birthdates on the back of the cards do not match the birthdates on the front of the cards and the fonts on the front and back do not match. The Appellant was asked to explain this at the hearing and he testified that he used what they sent him.29 The Appellant argues, as did counsel at the RPD, that there is no evidence such documents are uniform throughout the country and it is speculative to conclude that they are not authentic. I am not persuaded by this argument. I find that the Appellant has not addressed the discrepancies between the objective evidence on which the RPD relied and the evidence that the Appellant presented. I do not find it speculative to rely on independent evidence about documents. However, even if I were to accept, for purposes of the analysis, that the cards are not falsified, I find, for the reasons that follow, that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the support letters are genuine.

[19] The letter from XXXX states that after he and the Appellant were expelled from XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1993 they went their separate ways but still kept in contact with each other.30 The Appellant testified that he was able to get the letter from XXXX because he still had his contact information from almost 30 years ago but, asked if he had been in touch with XXXX before requesting the letter, the Appellant replied "No. No, no, no, no, no. No. No."31 Asked to explain why XXXX said they had kept contact, the Appellant changed his testimony to say they had kept contact for some time before they lost contact.32 The panel asked him when they lost contact and when they got back in contact and he replied that they lost contact after being expelled from XXXX XXXX but the Appellant kept his number and contacted him after coming to Canada in order to request a letter.33 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved and was inconsistent with the evidence in XXXX letter and that he did not reasonably explain the inconsistencies.

[20] The identity document accompanying the letter from XXXX uses the spelling "XXXX".34 This is an inconsistency between the spelling of XXXX name in a letter that XXXX allegedly wrote and signed and in the identity document accompanying his own letter. I find that the inconsistent spelling of the author's own name by the author himself undermines the credibility of the document.

[21] I have already addressed in paragraphs 8 to 9 the inconsistencies between the Appellant's evidence and the evidence in the letter from XXXX brother.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish that he is in a same-sex relationship in Canada, as alleged

[22] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence of a same-sex relationship in Canada with XXXX was not credible and that he did not establish the relationship, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant argues that this conclusion is incorrect. I agree with the Appellant that there are some errors in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. However, I find that the errors are not determinative and I find that the RPD's conclusion was correct. On an independent assessment, I reach the same conclusion, for the reasons that follow.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant provided inconsistent and vague evidence about the relationship

[23] The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about how he and XXXX met was inconsistent with his supporting evidence. He testified that they met in XXXX 2019 during a regular meeting at The XXXX Community Centre.35 The Appellant's evidence includes a letter from The XXXX which states that he registered for their newcomer orientation on XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020 and completed a needs intake with a settlement worker on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2020.36 Asked about this inconsistency, the Appellant testified that he was going there before he registered there.37 The panel did not find this to be a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. The letter does not indicate that the Appellant was attending the community centre in 2019 and it does not make sense that the Appellant would be attending regular meetings before attending an orientation session. The panel found that this undermined the credibility of the Appellant's evidence as to how he and XXXX met. The Appellant has not challenged this finding. I see no error in the panel's conclusion that the Appellant did not reasonably explain the inconsistency and that it undermines the credibility of his evidence that he and XXXX are same-sex partners.

[24] The RPD found that there were inconsistencies in the evidence given by the Appellant and by XXXX about how often they see each other. The Appellant testified that before COVID-19 they usually saw each other about twice a week, and now it was usually once a week.38 XXXX testified that before COVID-19 they used to meet every two weeks, and now it was every three weeks or up to a month.39 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies on the appeal although he argues, generally, that the RPD was overzealous in searching for inconsistencies and zeroed in on irrelevant details. I do not find these inconsistencies to be microscopic or irrelevant. The Appellant and XXXX gave significantly different accounts of how often they spent time together. I find that the discrepancies in their evidence undermine the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that they are same-sex partners.

[25] Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that their first date was at the Appellant's house and that he cooked a meal for them. Their evidence about the meal was inconsistent. The Appellant testified that they drank wine and he prepared XXXX favourite meal of givheri, a mixture with beans, and mboga, a cabbage dish.40 XXXX testified that they drank tea and the Appellant cooked meat and ugari.41 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies, specifically. I find that these inconsistencies, alone, would not be sufficient to conclude that the Appellant had not established the relationship, as alleged, but I have considered them in the context of the evidence as a whole.

[26] The RPD noted that the Appellant and XXXX were consistent in their testimony that they see one another at each other's homes, they both like to drink wine, the Appellant is the better cook, and they enjoy the same Kenyan music. As well, the Appellant's testimony was consistent with that of XXXX in describing how XXXX prefers his coffee. They both testified that they met at The XXXX in XXXX 2019. Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that XXXX works downtown doing maintenance for an apartment, and that he has three children and a wife in Kenya. I have considered this evidence and assessed it in the context of the totality of the evidence about the relationship.

[27] The RPD found that both the Appellant and XXXX were vague in their testimony as to what they like about each other and that their testimony fell short of what one would expect in describing a romantic partner. The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to apply the SOGIE Guideline.42 He argues that the RPD assumed that romantic relationships share the same dynamics and characteristics across culture. I am not persuaded by this argument. The RPD's finding was not based on the presence or absence of any particular dynamics or characteristics. It was based on the failure of the witnesses to provide evidence that would indicate that what each of them liked about the other was consistent with having been in an intimate relationship for about a year and a half. I see no error in the RPD's conclusion. I will explain.

[28] The RPD asked the Appellant what attracted him to XXXX. The Appellant testified that he was attracted to XXXX by his behaviour, his generosity and because he is good-hearted.43 I find this to be very general and lacking in any of the details or specificity that would reflect an intimate relationship of the duration alleged. XXXX was asked what he likes about the Appellant and he testified that the Appellant is a cool guy and is not very talkative, and that they like the same things, like music, and like to drink wine.44 I find that XXXX evidence would be sufficient to establish a superficial acquaintance or a friendship but does not indicate a more intimate relationship of a year and a half in length.
The RPD made errors in assessing the evidence of the relationship but they are not determinative

[29] The RPD found that the Appellant's description of how he got to XXXX house when visiting him was not credible. The Appellant gave XXXX address and stated that the house was a "few steps" from the subway station.45 The RPD referred to XXXX postal code as indicating that his house is a few kilometres away from any subway station and that the distance is therefore more than a "few steps". The Appellant argues that this is incorrect because a "few steps" can mean different things to different individuals. I accept the argument and find that the RPD erred. The Appellant's testimony was imprecise, there is no evidence in the record as to the distance from the closest subway station to XXXX house, and I find that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from this testimony. I accept that the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant knows where XXXX lives.

[30] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about his future relationship plans was inconsistent and vague. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by applying North American standards and stereotypical thinking. I find that the RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's evidence about future plans. The Appellant testified that, depending on their hearing outcomes, he and XXXX plan to move in together in the future.46 The Appellant also testified that, if his status in Canada changes, he will bring his wife to Canada and he intends to stay married to her.47 The RPD asked him how this would work and he testified that he and XXXX had agreed that they would have an arrangement about how they would meet.48 The panel found that the Appellant's evidence that he planned to live with XXXX and bring his wife to Canada was inconsistent and that his testimony about the future "arrangement" was vague.49 I find no inconsistency between the Appellant's evidence that he would move in with a partner in Canada and still bring his wife to Canada. His testimony was not that he would live with her; it was that he would bring her here and they would stay married. I accept the Appellant's argument that one can move in with a partner while staying married to one's wife. I also see no inconsistency between planning to live with her on arrival, and living with a partner here prior to her arrival, given that it can take many months, if not years, to bring a spouse to Canada. I also find that the Appellant's vagueness about an "arrangement" is not a basis for a negative inference. I find it reasonable that the Appellant would not have a clear plan about the conditions under which he would continue a same-sex relationship in Canada following his wife's arrival, particularly given that the Appellant has no assurance that he will be permitted to stay in Canada. I draw no inference from the Appellant's failure to specify the nature of the arrangement that he would make if his wife were to come to Canada.

[31] The RPD drew a negative inference from XXXX testimony that he did not know the names of the Appellant's children. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in concluding that it was reasonable to expect that XXXX would know the names of his children. I agree. I accept the Appellant's argument that it is plausible that the Appellant and XXXX would not discuss in detail previous relationships and children. XXXX testified that the Appellant had three children and he identified their ages.50 I draw no inference from XXXX lack of knowledge of the Appellant's children's names.

ANALYSIS

[5] The RPD found that the Appellant was generally not credible. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in assessing his credibility by being overzealous and microscopic and focusing on matters not central to his claim; by applying North American standards; by incorrectly concluding that there were inconsistencies and omissions between his testimony and the evidence in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC); and by incorrectly finding that supporting documents were non-genuine. While I find some errors in the RPD's assessment of the evidence, overall, I find that the panel did not err in concluding that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he is bisexual, as alleged. On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was generally not a credible witness. My reasons follow.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish the same-sex relationship with XXXX in Kenya, as alleged

[6] The RPD found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the same-sex relationship with XXXX in Kenya, as alleged. This finding was based on inconsistent evidence about the duration of the relationship and whether it was known to XXXX brother, as well as inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's description of the relationship. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by incorrectly characterizing as inconsistent the evidence describing the relationship and by incorrectly finding omissions. I am not persuaded by these arguments. I find that the RPD assessed the evidence correctly. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged. My reasons follow.

[7] The Appellant testified that he had a same-sex relationship with XXXX for about a year and a half.2 In subsequent testimony, he stated that the relationship began in 1996 and ended around 2006.3 Asked to explain the inconsistency in his testimony, the Appellant stated that the relationship was off and on and he cannot say what the duration was.4 The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. I agree. If the relationship was off and on over a period of ten years, this does not explain why the Appellant would testify that the relationship lasted for a year and a half. The Appellant has not taken issue with the RPD's finding on this inconsistency. I find no error in the RPD's conclusion that this is an inconsistency that undermines the credibility of the Appellant's evidence about this relationship.

[8] The Appellant provided a letter from XXXX brother to corroborate the relationship.5 The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with the letter. The Appellant's testimony was that XXXX died and XXXX brother contacted him to let him know.6 He testified XXXX brother knew that they were friends but never knew about their relationship.7 In the letter, XXXX brother states that, at XXXX send-off, the Appellant told him that they had a sexual relationship. Asked to explain why the brother would say that, the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Yeah, yeah. That one I did not want to use that one because I - I never - no - nobody told him that we had a sexual relationship, but during his send-off I remember I mentioned something like that to him.8
The panel asked the Appellant why he had previously testified that the brother did not know, and the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Because of how - how hard is in Kenya, when you declare yourself the sexual orientation that you are in like you are bisexual, I - I did not because of that fear. Maybe that is why I never told you before that I had told him - I - I had told him.9
The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation. I agree. The Appellant has not addressed this inconsistency in his arguments. I find no error in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. I have considered Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE Guideline).10 In particular, I have taken into account the challenges claimants may face in disclosing their sexual orientation, including psychological barriers. I do not find that this explains why the Appellant would testify at the RPD that the brother never knew about the relationship. The inconsistency that arose at the hearing was because he testified that he had not disclosed his relationship with XXXX to the brother.

[9] The brother's letter also states that XXXX died in a road accident in 2012. The Appellant testified that he found out about XXXX death in 2010.11 When questioned about the inconsistency, the Appellant testified that it might have been 2012.12 Given that the Appellant testified that he had attended the send-off, the panel asked him to explain, given the evidence that in 2012 he was in Afghanistan. The Appellant first said he was not in Afghanistan, then said that he was, and that every six months he was given a few days off and he would return to Nairobi.13 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved when he was confronted with inconsistencies between his testimony and other evidence and that this undermines his credibility as a witness.

[10] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about how he and XXXX spent time together was inconsistent. In his BOC, the Appellant's evidence is that they had a sexual relationship and they would rent rooms at hotels for sex or have sex in storage rooms at their workplace.14 The evidence in his BOC is that he was forced to resign his job because they were discovered together in a storage room.15 In his testimony, the Appellant said that he had a key to XXXX place, they used to hang out there together, they used to go to bars together, and they had a relationship.16 When the panel referred the Appellant to the evidence in his BOC and asked him why they would have sex at work or rent hotel rooms if they could go to XXXX place, the Appellant testified that it was for a change of atmosphere.17 The Appellant argues that there is no inconsistency in his evidence as his testimony constitutes elaborative details so it is incorrect to draw a negative credibility inference. He argues that the finding of inconsistency is based on the sparseness of the BOC and the style of the writing and it is an error to conclude that the Appellant described the relationship differently in his testimony. I am not persuaded by this argument. In his BOC, the Appellant described the relationship with XXXX as a sexual relationship that involved having sex at work. His testimony is that the relationship was more than a sexual one. I find this inconsistent. I also find his explanation that they rented hotel rooms for a change of atmosphere is not reasonable. However, if I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in finding this evidence inconsistent, for purposes of the analysis, I still conclude that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged, based on the findings that the Appellant has not challenged and that I have already discussed.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents

[11] The RPD found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in dismissing documents as non-genuine without considering what they say. I am not persuaded by this argument. The Federal Court has said that a letter that is not authentic has zero weight.18 The panel did not err in giving no weight to documents that were found to be non-genuine. On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant submitted documents that, on a balance of probabilities, are not genuine. My reasons follow.
The RPD correctly found that the school letters are not genuine documents

[12] The Appellant provided two letters in support of his allegation that he was expelled from two XXXX XXXX because, in each case, he was caught engaging in sexual activity with another male student. The RPD found that these letters were not authentic documents. On an independent assessment, I find no error in this and I reach the same conclusion. My reasons follow.

[13] The Appellant's evidence in his BOC was that in XXXX 1995 he was caught in sexual activity in an empty classroom, called to the principal's office on the same day, and expelled on the spot.19 In a letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 1995, the school principal states that he received a report on XXXX XXXX, 1995 on the Appellant's behaviour, he set up a panel with board members, the panel reached "an anonymous decision" to expel the Appellant, and the Appellant was "hereby expelled".20 Asked to explain the inconsistency between the letter and his BOC, the Appellant replied "Yeah, he - he expelled me on the spot, but it is after they met with [the] Board of Governors."21 The Appellant argues that he testified that he was expelled on the spot after the board of governors met. I do not accept this argument nor do I find his explanation for the inconsistency reasonable. It does not reasonably explain the discrepancy between the evidence in his BOC that he was called to the principal's office on the day he was caught and expelled on the spot, and the evidence in the letter that he was expelled two days later.

[14] The Appellant testified that he got the 1995 letter by contacting the school and he was lucky that they still had the record and agreed to give him the letter.22 He also presented a letter, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 1993, in support of his allegation that he was expelled from XXXX XXXX in 1993.23 The panel asked him how he got that letter and he testified that he has a friend who is a friend of the deputy principal and he was able to convince the principal to give the Appellant the letter.24 He was asked why the letter is dated in 1993 and he said it is because that was the year he left the school.25 I do not find it credible that a school principal would issue a letter, signing and stamping it with a date indicating that it was issued more than 25 years previously.

[15] The RPD found that the letters were, more likely than not, inauthentic. This finding was based on the inconsistency between the 1995 letter and the Appellant's evidence as well as the Appellant's evidence that he recently obtained these school letters bearing dates from more than twenty years ago. I find no error in the RPD's conclusion that both school letters are, on a balance of probabilities, not genuine.

[16] The Appellant argues that the 1995 letter supports the fact that he was expelled from school due to his same-sex sexual activity. I am not persuaded by this argument. Having found that the letter is not a genuine document, I give it no weight.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine support letters

[17] The RPD found that three of the support letters provided by the Appellant were likely not authentic because they were accompanied by identity documents that appeared to have been falsified. The Appellant argues that the documents should not be deemed fraudulent only because there is widespread forgery in the country from which the documents come. I agree, although the panel is entitled to consider the ease with which fraudulent documents can be obtained. However, in this case, the RPD made no reference to the prevalence of forged documents in Kenya. The finding was based on the documents themselves. On an independent assessment, I find that the support letters are, on a balance of probabilities, inauthentic. My reasons follow.

[18] The letters in question, with accompanying identity documents, are from the Appellant's alleged same-sex partners in XXXX XXXX, XXXX26 and XXXX,27 and the brother of his alleged same-sex partner XXXX .28 The RPD found that the identity cards differ from other identity cards provided and from samples in the objective evidence. The panel found that, on the three cards in question, the birthdates on the back of the cards do not match the birthdates on the front of the cards and the fonts on the front and back do not match. The Appellant was asked to explain this at the hearing and he testified that he used what they sent him.29 The Appellant argues, as did counsel at the RPD, that there is no evidence such documents are uniform throughout the country and it is speculative to conclude that they are not authentic. I am not persuaded by this argument. I find that the Appellant has not addressed the discrepancies between the objective evidence on which the RPD relied and the evidence that the Appellant presented. I do not find it speculative to rely on independent evidence about documents. However, even if I were to accept, for purposes of the analysis, that the cards are not falsified, I find, for the reasons that follow, that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the support letters are genuine.

[19] The letter from XXXX states that after he and the Appellant were expelled from XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1993 they went their separate ways but still kept in contact with each other.30 The Appellant testified that he was able to get the letter from XXXX because he still had his contact information from almost 30 years ago but, asked if he had been in touch with XXXX before requesting the letter, the Appellant replied "No. No, no, no, no, no. No. No."31 Asked to explain why XXXX said they had kept contact, the Appellant changed his testimony to say they had kept contact for some time before they lost contact.32 The panel asked him when they lost contact and when they got back in contact and he replied that they lost contact after being expelled from XXXX XXXX but the Appellant kept his number and contacted him after coming to Canada in order to request a letter.33 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved and was inconsistent with the evidence in XXXX letter and that he did not reasonably explain the inconsistencies.

[20] The identity document accompanying the letter from XXXX uses the spelling "XXXX".34 This is an inconsistency between the spelling of XXXX name in a letter that XXXX allegedly wrote and signed and in the identity document accompanying his own letter. I find that the inconsistent spelling of the author's own name by the author himself undermines the credibility of the document.

[21] I have already addressed in paragraphs 8 to 9 the inconsistencies between the Appellant's evidence and the evidence in the letter from XXXX brother.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish that he is in a same-sex relationship in Canada, as alleged

[22] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence of a same-sex relationship in Canada with XXXX was not credible and that he did not establish the relationship, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant argues that this conclusion is incorrect. I agree with the Appellant that there are some errors in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. However, I find that the errors are not determinative and I find that the RPD's conclusion was correct. On an independent assessment, I reach the same conclusion, for the reasons that follow.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant provided inconsistent and vague evidence about the relationship

[23] The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about how he and XXXX met was inconsistent with his supporting evidence. He testified that they met in XXXX 2019 during a regular meeting at The XXXX Community Centre.35 The Appellant's evidence includes a letter from The XXXX which states that he registered for their newcomer orientation on XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020 and completed a needs intake with a settlement worker on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2020.36 Asked about this inconsistency, the Appellant testified that he was going there before he registered there.37 The panel did not find this to be a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. The letter does not indicate that the Appellant was attending the community centre in 2019 and it does not make sense that the Appellant would be attending regular meetings before attending an orientation session. The panel found that this undermined the credibility of the Appellant's evidence as to how he and XXXX met. The Appellant has not challenged this finding. I see no error in the panel's conclusion that the Appellant did not reasonably explain the inconsistency and that it undermines the credibility of his evidence that he and XXXX are same-sex partners.

[24] The RPD found that there were inconsistencies in the evidence given by the Appellant and by XXXX about how often they see each other. The Appellant testified that before COVID-19 they usually saw each other about twice a week, and now it was usually once a week.38 XXXX testified that before COVID-19 they used to meet every two weeks, and now it was every three weeks or up to a month.39 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies on the appeal although he argues, generally, that the RPD was overzealous in searching for inconsistencies and zeroed in on irrelevant details. I do not find these inconsistencies to be microscopic or irrelevant. The Appellant and XXXX gave significantly different accounts of how often they spent time together. I find that the discrepancies in their evidence undermine the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that they are same-sex partners.

[25] Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that their first date was at the Appellant's house and that he cooked a meal for them. Their evidence about the meal was inconsistent. The Appellant testified that they drank wine and he prepared XXXX favourite meal of givheri, a mixture with beans, and mboga, a cabbage dish.40 XXXX testified that they drank tea and the Appellant cooked meat and ugari.41 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies, specifically. I find that these inconsistencies, alone, would not be sufficient to conclude that the Appellant had not established the relationship, as alleged, but I have considered them in the context of the evidence as a whole.

[26] The RPD noted that the Appellant and XXXX were consistent in their testimony that they see one another at each other's homes, they both like to drink wine, the Appellant is the better cook, and they enjoy the same Kenyan music. As well, the Appellant's testimony was consistent with that of XXXX in describing how XXXX prefers his coffee. They both testified that they met at The XXXX in XXXX 2019. Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that XXXX works downtown doing maintenance for an apartment, and that he has three children and a wife in Kenya. I have considered this evidence and assessed it in the context of the totality of the evidence about the relationship.

[27] The RPD found that both the Appellant and XXXX were vague in their testimony as to what they like about each other and that their testimony fell short of what one would expect in describing a romantic partner. The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to apply the SOGIE Guideline.42 He argues that the RPD assumed that romantic relationships share the same dynamics and characteristics across culture. I am not persuaded by this argument. The RPD's finding was not based on the presence or absence of any particular dynamics or characteristics. It was based on the failure of the witnesses to provide evidence that would indicate that what each of them liked about the other was consistent with having been in an intimate relationship for about a year and a half. I see no error in the RPD's conclusion. I will explain.

[28] The RPD asked the Appellant what attracted him to XXXX. The Appellant testified that he was attracted to XXXX by his behaviour, his generosity and because he is good-hearted.43 I find this to be very general and lacking in any of the details or specificity that would reflect an intimate relationship of the duration alleged. XXXX was asked what he likes about the Appellant and he testified that the Appellant is a cool guy and is not very talkative, and that they like the same things, like music, and like to drink wine.44 I find that XXXX evidence would be sufficient to establish a superficial acquaintance or a friendship but does not indicate a more intimate relationship of a year and a half in length.
The RPD made errors in assessing the evidence of the relationship but they are not determinative

[29] The RPD found that the Appellant's description of how he got to XXXX house when visiting him was not credible. The Appellant gave XXXX address and stated that the house was a "few steps" from the subway station.45 The RPD referred to XXXX postal code as indicating that his house is a few kilometres away from any subway station and that the distance is therefore more than a "few steps". The Appellant argues that this is incorrect because a "few steps" can mean different things to different individuals. I accept the argument and find that the RPD erred. The Appellant's testimony was imprecise, there is no evidence in the record as to the distance from the closest subway station to XXXX house, and I find that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from this testimony. I accept that the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant knows where XXXX lives.

[30] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about his future relationship plans was inconsistent and vague. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by applying North American standards and stereotypical thinking. I find that the RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's evidence about future plans. The Appellant testified that, depending on their hearing outcomes, he and XXXX plan to move in together in the future.46 The Appellant also testified that, if his status in Canada changes, he will bring his wife to Canada and he intends to stay married to her.47 The RPD asked him how this would work and he testified that he and XXXX had agreed that they would have an arrangement about how they would meet.48 The panel found that the Appellant's evidence that he planned to live with XXXX and bring his wife to Canada was inconsistent and that his testimony about the future "arrangement" was vague.49 I find no inconsistency between the Appellant's evidence that he would move in with a partner in Canada and still bring his wife to Canada. His testimony was not that he would live with her; it was that he would bring her here and they would stay married. I accept the Appellant's argument that one can move in with a partner while staying married to one's wife. I also see no inconsistency between planning to live with her on arrival, and living with a partner here prior to her arrival, given that it can take many months, if not years, to bring a spouse to Canada. I also find that the Appellant's vagueness about an "arrangement" is not a basis for a negative inference. I find it reasonable that the Appellant would not have a clear plan about the conditions under which he would continue a same-sex relationship in Canada following his wife's arrival, particularly given that the Appellant has no assurance that he will be permitted to stay in Canada. I draw no inference from the Appellant's failure to specify the nature of the arrangement that he would make if his wife were to come to Canada.

[31] The RPD drew a negative inference from XXXX testimony that he did not know the names of the Appellant's children. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in concluding that it was reasonable to expect that XXXX would know the names of his children. I agree. I accept the Appellant's argument that it is plausible that the Appellant and XXXX would not discuss in detail previous relationships and children. XXXX testified that the Appellant had three children and he identified their ages.50 I draw no inference from XXXX lack of knowledge of the Appellant's children's names.

CONCLUSION

[35] The Appellant's claim is based on his allegation that he is a bisexual man. He alleged same-sex relationships in Kenya and in Canada. He did not establish those relationships, on a balance of probabilities. He has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he is bisexual, as alleged. Consequently, he has not established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[36] I dismiss the appeal and, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act,53 confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who alleges that he fears persecution from his community and his family because of his sexual orientation as a bisexual man.

[2] The Appellant's claim was heard by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on March 12, 2021. The RPD rejected his claim on March 29, 2021. The determinative issue was credibility.
DECISION

[3] I dismiss the appeal. The determinative issue is credibility. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION
[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and independently determine whether the RPD made the correct decision.1
ANALYSIS

[5] The RPD found that the Appellant was generally not credible. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in assessing his credibility by being overzealous and microscopic and focusing on matters not central to his claim; by applying North American standards; by incorrectly concluding that there were inconsistencies and omissions between his testimony and the evidence in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC); and by incorrectly finding that supporting documents were non-genuine. While I find some errors in the RPD's assessment of the evidence, overall, I find that the panel did not err in concluding that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he is bisexual, as alleged. On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant was generally not a credible witness. My reasons follow.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish the same-sex relationship with XXXX in Kenya, as alleged

[6] The RPD found that the Appellant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the same-sex relationship with XXXX in Kenya, as alleged. This finding was based on inconsistent evidence about the duration of the relationship and whether it was known to XXXX brother, as well as inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's description of the relationship. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by incorrectly characterizing as inconsistent the evidence describing the relationship and by incorrectly finding omissions. I am not persuaded by these arguments. I find that the RPD assessed the evidence correctly. On an independent assessment, I find that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged. My reasons follow.

[7] The Appellant testified that he had a same-sex relationship with XXXX for about a year and a half.2 In subsequent testimony, he stated that the relationship began in 1996 and ended around 2006.3 Asked to explain the inconsistency in his testimony, the Appellant stated that the relationship was off and on and he cannot say what the duration was.4 The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. I agree. If the relationship was off and on over a period of ten years, this does not explain why the Appellant would testify that the relationship lasted for a year and a half. The Appellant has not taken issue with the RPD's finding on this inconsistency. I find no error in the RPD's conclusion that this is an inconsistency that undermines the credibility of the Appellant's evidence about this relationship.

[8] The Appellant provided a letter from XXXX brother to corroborate the relationship.5 The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with the letter. The Appellant's testimony was that XXXX died and XXXX brother contacted him to let him know.6 He testified XXXX brother knew that they were friends but never knew about their relationship.7 In the letter, XXXX brother states that, at XXXX send-off, the Appellant told him that they had a sexual relationship. Asked to explain why the brother would say that, the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Yeah, yeah. That one I did not want to use that one because I - I never - no - nobody told him that we had a sexual relationship, but during his send-off I remember I mentioned something like that to him.8
The panel asked the Appellant why he had previously testified that the brother did not know, and the Appellant replied:
CLAIMANT: Because of how - how hard is in Kenya, when you declare yourself the sexual orientation that you are in like you are bisexual, I - I did not because of that fear. Maybe that is why I never told you before that I had told him - I - I had told him.9
The RPD found that this was not a reasonable explanation. I agree. The Appellant has not addressed this inconsistency in his arguments. I find no error in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. I have considered Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE Guideline).10 In particular, I have taken into account the challenges claimants may face in disclosing their sexual orientation, including psychological barriers. I do not find that this explains why the Appellant would testify at the RPD that the brother never knew about the relationship. The inconsistency that arose at the hearing was because he testified that he had not disclosed his relationship with XXXX to the brother.

[9] The brother's letter also states that XXXX died in a road accident in 2012. The Appellant testified that he found out about XXXX death in 2010.11 When questioned about the inconsistency, the Appellant testified that it might have been 2012.12 Given that the Appellant testified that he had attended the send-off, the panel asked him to explain, given the evidence that in 2012 he was in Afghanistan. The Appellant first said he was not in Afghanistan, then said that he was, and that every six months he was given a few days off and he would return to Nairobi.13 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved when he was confronted with inconsistencies between his testimony and other evidence and that this undermines his credibility as a witness.

[10] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about how he and XXXX spent time together was inconsistent. In his BOC, the Appellant's evidence is that they had a sexual relationship and they would rent rooms at hotels for sex or have sex in storage rooms at their workplace.14 The evidence in his BOC is that he was forced to resign his job because they were discovered together in a storage room.15 In his testimony, the Appellant said that he had a key to XXXX place, they used to hang out there together, they used to go to bars together, and they had a relationship.16 When the panel referred the Appellant to the evidence in his BOC and asked him why they would have sex at work or rent hotel rooms if they could go to XXXX place, the Appellant testified that it was for a change of atmosphere.17 The Appellant argues that there is no inconsistency in his evidence as his testimony constitutes elaborative details so it is incorrect to draw a negative credibility inference. He argues that the finding of inconsistency is based on the sparseness of the BOC and the style of the writing and it is an error to conclude that the Appellant described the relationship differently in his testimony. I am not persuaded by this argument. In his BOC, the Appellant described the relationship with XXXX as a sexual relationship that involved having sex at work. His testimony is that the relationship was more than a sexual one. I find this inconsistent. I also find his explanation that they rented hotel rooms for a change of atmosphere is not reasonable. However, if I accept the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in finding this evidence inconsistent, for purposes of the analysis, I still conclude that the Appellant has not established the relationship with XXXX, as alleged, based on the findings that the Appellant has not challenged and that I have already discussed.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents

[11] The RPD found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine documents. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in dismissing documents as non-genuine without considering what they say. I am not persuaded by this argument. The Federal Court has said that a letter that is not authentic has zero weight.18 The panel did not err in giving no weight to documents that were found to be non-genuine. On an independent assessment, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant submitted documents that, on a balance of probabilities, are not genuine. My reasons follow.
The RPD correctly found that the school letters are not genuine documents

[12] The Appellant provided two letters in support of his allegation that he was expelled from two XXXX XXXX because, in each case, he was caught engaging in sexual activity with another male student. The RPD found that these letters were not authentic documents. On an independent assessment, I find no error in this and I reach the same conclusion. My reasons follow.

[13] The Appellant's evidence in his BOC was that in XXXX 1995 he was caught in sexual activity in an empty classroom, called to the principal's office on the same day, and expelled on the spot.19 In a letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 1995, the school principal states that he received a report on XXXX XXXX, 1995 on the Appellant's behaviour, he set up a panel with board members, the panel reached "an anonymous decision" to expel the Appellant, and the Appellant was "hereby expelled".20 Asked to explain the inconsistency between the letter and his BOC, the Appellant replied "Yeah, he - he expelled me on the spot, but it is after they met with [the] Board of Governors."21 The Appellant argues that he testified that he was expelled on the spot after the board of governors met. I do not accept this argument nor do I find his explanation for the inconsistency reasonable. It does not reasonably explain the discrepancy between the evidence in his BOC that he was called to the principal's office on the day he was caught and expelled on the spot, and the evidence in the letter that he was expelled two days later.

[14] The Appellant testified that he got the 1995 letter by contacting the school and he was lucky that they still had the record and agreed to give him the letter.22 He also presented a letter, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 1993, in support of his allegation that he was expelled from XXXX XXXX in 1993.23 The panel asked him how he got that letter and he testified that he has a friend who is a friend of the deputy principal and he was able to convince the principal to give the Appellant the letter.24 He was asked why the letter is dated in 1993 and he said it is because that was the year he left the school.25 I do not find it credible that a school principal would issue a letter, signing and stamping it with a date indicating that it was issued more than 25 years previously.

[15] The RPD found that the letters were, more likely than not, inauthentic. This finding was based on the inconsistency between the 1995 letter and the Appellant's evidence as well as the Appellant's evidence that he recently obtained these school letters bearing dates from more than twenty years ago. I find no error in the RPD's conclusion that both school letters are, on a balance of probabilities, not genuine.

[16] The Appellant argues that the 1995 letter supports the fact that he was expelled from school due to his same-sex sexual activity. I am not persuaded by this argument. Having found that the letter is not a genuine document, I give it no weight.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant submitted non-genuine support letters

[17] The RPD found that three of the support letters provided by the Appellant were likely not authentic because they were accompanied by identity documents that appeared to have been falsified. The Appellant argues that the documents should not be deemed fraudulent only because there is widespread forgery in the country from which the documents come. I agree, although the panel is entitled to consider the ease with which fraudulent documents can be obtained. However, in this case, the RPD made no reference to the prevalence of forged documents in Kenya. The finding was based on the documents themselves. On an independent assessment, I find that the support letters are, on a balance of probabilities, inauthentic. My reasons follow.

[18] The letters in question, with accompanying identity documents, are from the Appellant's alleged same-sex partners in XXXX XXXX, XXXX26 and XXXX,27 and the brother of his alleged same-sex partner XXXX .28 The RPD found that the identity cards differ from other identity cards provided and from samples in the objective evidence. The panel found that, on the three cards in question, the birthdates on the back of the cards do not match the birthdates on the front of the cards and the fonts on the front and back do not match. The Appellant was asked to explain this at the hearing and he testified that he used what they sent him.29 The Appellant argues, as did counsel at the RPD, that there is no evidence such documents are uniform throughout the country and it is speculative to conclude that they are not authentic. I am not persuaded by this argument. I find that the Appellant has not addressed the discrepancies between the objective evidence on which the RPD relied and the evidence that the Appellant presented. I do not find it speculative to rely on independent evidence about documents. However, even if I were to accept, for purposes of the analysis, that the cards are not falsified, I find, for the reasons that follow, that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the support letters are genuine.

[19] The letter from XXXX states that after he and the Appellant were expelled from XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1993 they went their separate ways but still kept in contact with each other.30 The Appellant testified that he was able to get the letter from XXXX because he still had his contact information from almost 30 years ago but, asked if he had been in touch with XXXX before requesting the letter, the Appellant replied "No. No, no, no, no, no. No. No."31 Asked to explain why XXXX said they had kept contact, the Appellant changed his testimony to say they had kept contact for some time before they lost contact.32 The panel asked him when they lost contact and when they got back in contact and he replied that they lost contact after being expelled from XXXX XXXX but the Appellant kept his number and contacted him after coming to Canada in order to request a letter.33 I find that the Appellant's testimony evolved and was inconsistent with the evidence in XXXX letter and that he did not reasonably explain the inconsistencies.

[20] The identity document accompanying the letter from XXXX uses the spelling "XXXX".34 This is an inconsistency between the spelling of XXXX name in a letter that XXXX allegedly wrote and signed and in the identity document accompanying his own letter. I find that the inconsistent spelling of the author's own name by the author himself undermines the credibility of the document.

[21] I have already addressed in paragraphs 8 to 9 the inconsistencies between the Appellant's evidence and the evidence in the letter from XXXX brother.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant did not establish that he is in a same-sex relationship in Canada, as alleged

[22] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence of a same-sex relationship in Canada with XXXX was not credible and that he did not establish the relationship, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant argues that this conclusion is incorrect. I agree with the Appellant that there are some errors in the RPD's assessment of the evidence. However, I find that the errors are not determinative and I find that the RPD's conclusion was correct. On an independent assessment, I reach the same conclusion, for the reasons that follow.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant provided inconsistent and vague evidence about the relationship

[23] The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about how he and XXXX met was inconsistent with his supporting evidence. He testified that they met in XXXX 2019 during a regular meeting at The XXXX Community Centre.35 The Appellant's evidence includes a letter from The XXXX which states that he registered for their newcomer orientation on XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020 and completed a needs intake with a settlement worker on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2020.36 Asked about this inconsistency, the Appellant testified that he was going there before he registered there.37 The panel did not find this to be a reasonable explanation for the inconsistency. The letter does not indicate that the Appellant was attending the community centre in 2019 and it does not make sense that the Appellant would be attending regular meetings before attending an orientation session. The panel found that this undermined the credibility of the Appellant's evidence as to how he and XXXX met. The Appellant has not challenged this finding. I see no error in the panel's conclusion that the Appellant did not reasonably explain the inconsistency and that it undermines the credibility of his evidence that he and XXXX are same-sex partners.

[24] The RPD found that there were inconsistencies in the evidence given by the Appellant and by XXXX about how often they see each other. The Appellant testified that before COVID-19 they usually saw each other about twice a week, and now it was usually once a week.38 XXXX testified that before COVID-19 they used to meet every two weeks, and now it was every three weeks or up to a month.39 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies on the appeal although he argues, generally, that the RPD was overzealous in searching for inconsistencies and zeroed in on irrelevant details. I do not find these inconsistencies to be microscopic or irrelevant. The Appellant and XXXX gave significantly different accounts of how often they spent time together. I find that the discrepancies in their evidence undermine the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that they are same-sex partners.

[25] Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that their first date was at the Appellant's house and that he cooked a meal for them. Their evidence about the meal was inconsistent. The Appellant testified that they drank wine and he prepared XXXX favourite meal of givheri, a mixture with beans, and mboga, a cabbage dish.40 XXXX testified that they drank tea and the Appellant cooked meat and ugari.41 The Appellant has not addressed these inconsistencies, specifically. I find that these inconsistencies, alone, would not be sufficient to conclude that the Appellant had not established the relationship, as alleged, but I have considered them in the context of the evidence as a whole.

[26] The RPD noted that the Appellant and XXXX were consistent in their testimony that they see one another at each other's homes, they both like to drink wine, the Appellant is the better cook, and they enjoy the same Kenyan music. As well, the Appellant's testimony was consistent with that of XXXX in describing how XXXX prefers his coffee. They both testified that they met at The XXXX in XXXX 2019. Both the Appellant and XXXX testified that XXXX works downtown doing maintenance for an apartment, and that he has three children and a wife in Kenya. I have considered this evidence and assessed it in the context of the totality of the evidence about the relationship.

[27] The RPD found that both the Appellant and XXXX were vague in their testimony as to what they like about each other and that their testimony fell short of what one would expect in describing a romantic partner. The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to apply the SOGIE Guideline.42 He argues that the RPD assumed that romantic relationships share the same dynamics and characteristics across culture. I am not persuaded by this argument. The RPD's finding was not based on the presence or absence of any particular dynamics or characteristics. It was based on the failure of the witnesses to provide evidence that would indicate that what each of them liked about the other was consistent with having been in an intimate relationship for about a year and a half. I see no error in the RPD's conclusion. I will explain.

[28] The RPD asked the Appellant what attracted him to XXXX. The Appellant testified that he was attracted to XXXX by his behaviour, his generosity and because he is good-hearted.43 I find this to be very general and lacking in any of the details or specificity that would reflect an intimate relationship of the duration alleged. XXXX was asked what he likes about the Appellant and he testified that the Appellant is a cool guy and is not very talkative, and that they like the same things, like music, and like to drink wine.44 I find that XXXX evidence would be sufficient to establish a superficial acquaintance or a friendship but does not indicate a more intimate relationship of a year and a half in length.
The RPD made errors in assessing the evidence of the relationship but they are not determinative

[29] The RPD found that the Appellant's description of how he got to XXXX house when visiting him was not credible. The Appellant gave XXXX address and stated that the house was a "few steps" from the subway station.45 The RPD referred to XXXX postal code as indicating that his house is a few kilometres away from any subway station and that the distance is therefore more than a "few steps". The Appellant argues that this is incorrect because a "few steps" can mean different things to different individuals. I accept the argument and find that the RPD erred. The Appellant's testimony was imprecise, there is no evidence in the record as to the distance from the closest subway station to XXXX house, and I find that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from this testimony. I accept that the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant knows where XXXX lives.

[30] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about his future relationship plans was inconsistent and vague. The Appellant argues that the panel erred by applying North American standards and stereotypical thinking. I find that the RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's evidence about future plans. The Appellant testified that, depending on their hearing outcomes, he and XXXX plan to move in together in the future.46 The Appellant also testified that, if his status in Canada changes, he will bring his wife to Canada and he intends to stay married to her.47 The RPD asked him how this would work and he testified that he and XXXX had agreed that they would have an arrangement about how they would meet.48 The panel found that the Appellant's evidence that he planned to live with XXXX and bring his wife to Canada was inconsistent and that his testimony about the future "arrangement" was vague.49 I find no inconsistency between the Appellant's evidence that he would move in with a partner in Canada and still bring his wife to Canada. His testimony was not that he would live with her; it was that he would bring her here and they would stay married. I accept the Appellant's argument that one can move in with a partner while staying married to one's wife. I also see no inconsistency between planning to live with her on arrival, and living with a partner here prior to her arrival, given that it can take many months, if not years, to bring a spouse to Canada. I also find that the Appellant's vagueness about an "arrangement" is not a basis for a negative inference. I find it reasonable that the Appellant would not have a clear plan about the conditions under which he would continue a same-sex relationship in Canada following his wife's arrival, particularly given that the Appellant has no assurance that he will be permitted to stay in Canada. I draw no inference from the Appellant's failure to specify the nature of the arrangement that he would make if his wife were to come to Canada.

[31] The RPD drew a negative inference from XXXX testimony that he did not know the names of the Appellant's children. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in concluding that it was reasonable to expect that XXXX would know the names of his children. I agree. I accept the Appellant's argument that it is plausible that the Appellant and XXXX would not discuss in detail previous relationships and children. XXXX testified that the Appellant had three children and he identified their ages.50 I draw no inference from XXXX lack of knowledge of the Appellant's children's names.

[32] I find that these errors are non-determinative. The RPD relied on other aspects of the Appellant's evidence in concluding that he failed to establish his relationship with XXXX, as alleged. Furthermore, it is the role of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to assess the evidence independently. I find that, on doing so, for the reasons I have given, I conclude that the Appellant has not established the alleged relationship, on a balance of probabilities.
The RPD correctly found that the Appellant was wholly not credible

[33] The RPD found that the Appellant lost the presumption of truthfulness, owing to inconsistencies in his evidence. His credibility was further undermined by the use of non-genuine documents. I have explained why I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant failed to establish specific allegations. The Federal Court has found that the cumulative effect of credibility concerns can lead to the conclusion that a claimant's credibility is fatally undermined.51 This is the conclusion I have reached regarding the Appellant.

[34] In reaching this conclusion, I considered the psychotherapist's report.52 The Appellant was diagnosed by his physician with XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and was referred for a psychotherapy assessment. Symptoms that the Appellant reported to the psychotherapist included difficulty focusing and remembering things. The Appellant has not argued that the evidence in the psychotherapist's report explains inconsistencies and omissions in his evidence. Furthermore, the evidence in the report cannot explain the issues with the Appellant's supporting documents. I find that, taking into account the psychotherapist's report, I reach the same conclusion. The Appellant is not a credible witness.
CONCLUSION

[35] The Appellant's claim is based on his allegation that he is a bisexual man. He alleged same-sex relationships in Kenya and in Canada. He did not establish those relationships, on a balance of probabilities. He has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he is bisexual, as alleged. Consequently, he has not established that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[36] I dismiss the appeal and, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act,53 confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
